title: JOSEPH NAMED HIS FIRST SON “GOD HAS MADE ME FORGET”—WHAT WAS HE TRYING TO LEAVE BEHIND?
paragraphs: JOSEPH NAMED HIS FIRST SON “GOD HAS MADE ME FORGET”—WHAT WAS HE TRYING TO LEAVE BEHIND?
His brothers sold him. His master’s wife accused him. His friends forgot him. Then Joseph gave his firstborn a name that revealed what success could never erase.
There are some things you survive…
but somehow, they keep surviving inside you.
You leave the house where it happened.
You stop talking to the person who hurt you.
Years pass.
Your circumstances change.
You learn how to smile again.
People look at you and think you are doing fine.
Maybe you even become successful.
But sometimes all it takes is a name.
A place.
A smell.
A familiar voice.
A certain date on the calendar.
And suddenly the person you thought you had buried inside yesterday starts breathing again.
Joseph knew something about that.
Before he wore fine linen in Egypt, he wore the clothes of a prisoner.
Before Pharaoh placed a gold chain around his neck, iron had known his body.
Before people bowed before him, people had thrown him away.
Before Joseph became powerful enough to command a nation, he had been powerless enough to hear his own brothers discussing what to do with him.
And when Joseph finally had a son, he did something extraordinary.
He turned his child’s name into a testimony.
Genesis 41:50–52 tells us:
“Unto Joseph were born two sons before the years of famine came…”
Joseph named the firstborn Manasseh.
The Hebrew text says:
וַיִּקְרָא יוֹסֵף אֶת־שֵׁם הַבְּכוֹר מְנַשֶּׁה כִּי־נַשַּׁנִי אֱלֹהִים אֶת־כָּל־עֲמָלִי וְאֵת כָּל־בֵּית אָבִי
Vayyiqra Yosef et-shem habbekhor Menashsheh, ki-nashshani Elohim et-kol-amali ve'et kol-beit avi.
The sense is:
Joseph called his firstborn Manasseh, saying, “God has made me forget all my hardship and all my father’s house.”
Then he named his second son Ephraim, because, as Joseph declared:
כִּי־הִפְרַנִי אֱלֹהִים בְּאֶרֶץ עָנְיִי
Ki-hifrani Elohim be'eretz onyi.
“For God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Do not rush past those names.
Manasseh.
God has made me forget.
Ephraim.
God has made me fruitful.
Forget.
Then fruitful.
Pain.
Then purpose.
Affliction.
Then abundance.
But what exactly was Joseph trying to forget?
Because Joseph had not forgotten the facts.
We know that.
Years later, when his brothers appeared before him, Joseph recognized them.
He remembered.
He remembered his father.
He remembered his younger brother Benjamin.
He remembered the dreams of his youth.
Genesis 42:9 explicitly says:
“And Joseph remembered the dreams which he dreamed of them.”
So when Joseph said God had caused him to “forget,” Scripture cannot reasonably mean that God erased Joseph’s memory like deleting a file.
Joseph remembered.
What changed was the power those memories possessed over his present life.
And maybe that is exactly where this story finds you.
Because perhaps you have been asking God to make you forget something He intends to redeem.
You have prayed:
“Lord, just take the memory away.”
But it remains.
You still remember what they said.
You remember who walked away.
You remember the betrayal.
You remember the funeral.
You remember the message you discovered.
You remember the humiliation.
You remember the night everything changed.
You remember who you were before the addiction.
Before the divorce.
Before the betrayal.
Before the failure.
Before your family fractured.
Before your faith became complicated.
Before you learned that people you trusted could wound you.
And because you still remember, perhaps you have wondered whether God has actually healed you.
Joseph’s story whispers something different.
Healing is not always the absence of memory. Sometimes healing is when the memory remains, but it no longer owns you.
Joseph was not pretending the pit never happened.
He was declaring that the pit would no longer determine who he became.
Think about what was behind him.
His brothers hated him.
Genesis 37 tells us they could not speak peaceably to him.
They stripped away the special garment his father had given him.
They threw him into a pit.
Then they sat down to eat.
That detail hurts.
Joseph was in the pit while his brothers were having a meal.
Eventually they sold him.
A human being.
Their own brother.
Twenty pieces of silver.
Then Joseph was carried into Egypt.
Imagine the journey.
Every mile taking him farther from home.
Every step reinforcing the same terrible reality:
Nobody is coming.
His father did not know where he was.
His brothers were responsible for his disappearance.
His old life was gone.
Then Joseph served in Potiphar’s house.
He acted faithfully.
God was with him.
Things began improving.
And then another betrayal came.
Potiphar’s wife repeatedly tried to seduce Joseph.
Joseph refused.
His reasoning was not merely social.
It was theological.
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” he said in Genesis 39:9.
Joseph ran from sexual sin.
And what did righteousness get him?
Prison.
She falsely accused him.
The innocent man was punished.
Joseph had done the right thing…
and still suffered.
Someone reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
You obeyed God and still lost something.
You told the truth and people believed the lie.
You remained faithful and somebody betrayed you.
You tried to honor Christ and watched someone who compromised appear to prosper.
There are seasons when obedience does not immediately look like victory.
Joseph teaches us that the absence of immediate vindication is not the absence of God.
Genesis 39 repeatedly emphasizes that the LORD was with Joseph.
In the house.
In the injustice.
In the prison.
God was there.
That changes the way we understand suffering.
Joseph was not abandoned in the pit.
He was not abandoned in slavery.
He was not abandoned when falsely accused.
He was not abandoned behind prison walls.
And neither the pit nor the palace was ultimately the center of Joseph’s story.
God was.
Then came another wound.
Joseph interpreted the cupbearer’s dream and asked him to remember him before Pharaoh.
Genesis 40:23 delivers one of Scripture’s painfully understated sentences:
“Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgat him.”
Forgotten.
Again.
First rejected by his brothers.
Then falsely accused.
Then forgotten by someone he had helped.
Two more years passed.
Imagine those years.
No Genesis 41 yet.
No Pharaoh calling.
No chariot.
No promotion.
Just prison walls and a promise that seemed increasingly difficult to understand.
But then Pharaoh dreamed.
And suddenly the man forgotten in prison became the man Egypt desperately needed.
Joseph was brought before Pharaoh.
God gave him wisdom.
Joseph interpreted the dreams.
Pharaoh recognized extraordinary wisdom in him and elevated Joseph over Egypt.
In one breathtaking reversal, the prisoner became governor.
But then Joseph had a child.
And suddenly we discover that underneath the Egyptian clothing, underneath the authority, underneath the success…
there was still a man remembering where he came from.
So he named the boy Manasseh.
“God has made me forget…”
Perhaps Joseph was saying:
God has carried me beyond the season that once defined my entire world.
God has loosened suffering’s grip on me.
God has given me a life beyond the life I thought had been destroyed.
God has shown me that what happened to me does not have to become what rules me.
But there is another detail that makes this even more powerful.
Joseph did not stop with Manasseh.
His second son was Ephraim.
“God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Not after the land of affliction.
In it.
That changes everything.
Joseph did not need to return to Canaan before he could become fruitful.
God produced fruit in Egypt.
The place associated with Joseph’s displacement became the place where God demonstrated His provision.
Maybe you keep telling yourself:
“When this season ends, I can live again.”
“When the pain disappears, I can serve God again.”
“When my family changes, I can have peace.”
“When someone apologizes, I can heal.”
“When God explains everything, I will trust Him.”
Joseph’s life confronts that thinking.
God can make you fruitful in the land of your affliction.
The place you would never have chosen may become the place where you discover dimensions of God you would never have known otherwise.
That does not make evil good.
The Bible never requires us to rename betrayal as goodness.
Joseph’s brothers sinned.
The false accusation was wrong.
The injustice was real.
The suffering mattered.
Biblical forgiveness is not pretending evil was acceptable.
And Joseph’s later words prove it.
Years after naming Manasseh, Joseph stood before the same brothers who sold him.
Now Joseph had power.
They did not.
He could finally make them feel what he had felt.
This was the moment revenge had been waiting for.
But grace had rewritten the man.
Joseph wept.
Eventually he revealed himself.
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine what those words did to that room.
The brother they discarded was alive.
The slave had become ruler.
The victim now possessed enormous power over the people who victimized him.
And yet Joseph could see something larger than revenge.
Genesis 50:20 records his famous words:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
Notice carefully what Joseph did not say.
He did not say:
“What you did was good.”
He said:
You meant evil.
Joseph called evil what it was.
But then he declared that human evil did not possess the final word.
God meant it unto good.
That is biblical redemption.
Not pretending the wound never happened.
Not calling darkness light.
Not denying injustice.
But discovering that sinful people cannot outmaneuver a sovereign God.
They may write a terrible chapter.
They do not get to write the ending.
And this is where Joseph’s story begins pointing beyond Joseph.
Because there would come another beloved Son.
Jesus Christ.
Rejected by His own.
Betrayed for silver.
Falsely accused.
Mocked.
Stripped.
Condemned though innocent.
And crucified.
At Calvary, human wickedness appeared to have reached its triumph.
The Messiah hung on a cross.
His body was broken.
His blood was shed.
He died.
He was buried.
For a moment, it looked as though darkness had written the final sentence.
Then came Sunday.
The stone was rolled away.
Christ rose from the dead.
And the cross—the instrument meant for shame and death—became the place where God displayed redemption.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
We are not merely wounded people needing emotional improvement.
We are sinners needing reconciliation with a holy God.
Our greatest problem is deeper than what people have done to us.
It is the sin within us that separates us from God.
And Jesus did not come merely to make our lives easier.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He died.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is offered through Him.
Grace does not tell you that your sin does not matter.
Grace tells you that your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is greater than the guilt you bring to Him.
Maybe the hardest thing you need to leave behind is not what somebody did to you.
Maybe it is what you did.
The secret.
The compromise.
The pornography nobody knows about.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The years you wasted.
The person you hurt.
The faith you abandoned.
The prayer life you neglected.
The version of yourself you are ashamed to remember.
You cannot save yourself by forgetting it.
You cannot heal yourself by hiding it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Repentance does not mean pretending yesterday never happened.
It means turning from sin and turning toward Christ.
And the Gospel announces something breathtaking:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus Christ specializes in resurrection.
Peter denied Him and was restored.
Paul persecuted the church and became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The thief beside Jesus had nothing left to offer—no years of ministry, no opportunity to repair his reputation, no lifetime of religious accomplishments.
He had only a dying prayer:
“Lord, remember me…”
And Jesus gave him paradise.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never existed.
By overwhelming it with grace.
Maybe that is why Manasseh matters so much.
Joseph could hold his son and realize:
“I have a future.”
The pit told him his story was over.
Manasseh said otherwise.
The chains said his identity was prisoner.
Manasseh said otherwise.
The accusation said his reputation was destroyed.
Manasseh said otherwise.
The forgotten years said nothing was changing.
Manasseh said otherwise.
Then Joseph could hold Ephraim and say:
“I am not merely surviving anymore.
God is producing fruit here.”
Maybe today you need your own Manasseh moment.
Not amnesia.
Surrender.
You need to stop visiting an old wound every morning and asking it who you are.
You need to stop allowing the person who rejected you to continue controlling your identity years after they walked away.
You need to stop rehearsing the accusation Christ has already answered with His blood.
You need to stop building a permanent home inside a chapter God intended you to walk through.
And perhaps you need an Ephraim moment too.
You need to believe that God can still produce something beautiful in a life that has been painfully interrupted.
Listen carefully:
You are not required to forget the facts in order to be free from their mastery.
Joseph remembered.
But he was no longer living in the pit.
And there is something else Joseph’s story teaches us.
Years later, the very brothers connected to his pain would stand before him needing bread.
Joseph’s suffering had somehow placed him where he could preserve lives.
That does not justify what they did.
It reveals what God can do despite it.
Your scars may someday speak to somebody still bleeding.
Your testimony may become somebody else’s reason not to give up.
The season you begged God to erase may eventually become the story through which another wounded person discovers Jesus.
So do not waste your pain.
Give it to Christ.
Let Him redeem what you cannot rewrite yourself.
And if this exposed something you have kept buried, do not hide behind religious language today.
Be honest.
You do not have to explain everything publicly.
Sometimes two or three honest words are enough to say, “I am still fighting. I still believe God is not finished with me.”
And read the other comments.
You may discover that the person beside you in this digital room has been carrying a wound that looks remarkably like yours.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Remind them of Christ.
That is what the body of Christ should do.
They may never tell you.
They may never comment.
They may look completely fine.
But perhaps the message God places before them through your simple share will remind them to look toward Jesus again.
There are truths you understand differently when the wound starts speaking again.
Come back when yesterday feels louder than grace.
Come back and remember Joseph.
Manasseh.
Ephraim.
The pit.
The prison.
The palace.
And above all…
the God who was present through all of it.
Scripture says giving should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
That matters to us.
We do not want fear to make your decision.
We do not want guilt to make your decision.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Your support helps us keep going.
Your sharing helps us reach farther.
Your prayers matter.
Your participation matters.
And when believers freely use what God has entrusted to them to support Gospel-centered work, that generosity can become an act of worship offered to God.
And comment.
Tell us what God is doing.
Tell us what you are fighting.
Tell us what you are surrendering.
Tell us what Christ has already brought you through.
Because someone else may read your testimony and realize they are not alone.
Joseph called his first son Manasseh.
“God has made me forget.”
Then came Ephraim.
“God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
Maybe your Manasseh is not God erasing your memory.
Maybe it is God breaking your memory’s authority over you.
Maybe your Ephraim is not escaping every painful circumstance.
Maybe it is discovering that Christ can produce fruit even there.
And maybe one day you will look back at the chapter you thought would destroy you and realize something that Joseph eventually understood:
People wounded you.
Sin scarred you.
Life changed you.
But none of them possessed the pen.
Jesus Christ still does.
So bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the memory you cannot erase.
Bring Him your sin in repentance.
Bring Him your wounded heart in faith.
And let the Savior who walked out of His own grave show you what He can do with things everyone else thought were finished.
Because perhaps the miracle is not that one day you will remember nothing.
Perhaps the miracle is that one day you will remember everything…
and discover that the wound no longer gets to tell you who you are.
